{{Short description|1666 scientific book by Gottfried Leibniz}}
{{Title language|la}}
{{Use Oxford spelling |date=September 2025}}
{{Use dmy dates |date=September 2025}}
[[File:Fotothek_df_tg_0005486_Mathematik_%5E_Kombinatorik.jpg|thumb|right|300 px|Frontispiece of the book printed in 1690]]
The {{lang |la |Dissertatio '''De Arte Combinatoria'''}} ({{gloss |Dissertation on the Art of Combinations}} or {{gloss |Dissertation on the Combinatorial Art}}) is an early work by [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Gottfried Leibniz]] published in 1666 in [[Leipzig]].{{sfnp|Leibniz|1923|p=163}}{{sfnp|Gerhardt|loc=volume 4|p=30}} It is an extended version of his first [[doctoral dissertation]],{{efn |The first part of the book was his [[doctoral thesis]] in Philosophy at [[Leipzig University]]. Leibniz defended his thesis in March 1666.{{sfnp|Arthur|2014|p=x}}}} written before the author had seriously undertaken the study of mathematics.{{sfnp|Leibniz|1966|p=32}} The booklet was reissued without Leibniz' consent in 1690, which prompted him to publish a brief explanatory notice in the {{lang |la |[[Acta Eruditorum]]}}.{{sfnp|Leibniz|1691|pp=63–64}} During the following years he repeatedly expressed regrets about its being circulated as he considered it immature.{{efn |Leibniz complained to various correspondents such as Morell (1 October 1697) and Meier (23 January 1699).{{sfnp|Akademie|loc=I.14|p=548}}{{sfnp|Akademie|loc=I.16|p=540}}}} Nevertheless it was a very original work and it provided the author the first glimpse of fame among the scholars of his time.

The book was created as part of Leibniz's efforts to create the {{lang |la |[[Characteristica Universalis]]}}, the [[perfect language]] which would provide a direct representation of ideas along with a [[Calculus ratiocinator|calculus for the philosophical reasoning]].

==Summary==
The main idea behind the text is that of an [[alphabet of human thought]], which is attributed to [[Descartes]]. All concepts are nothing but [[combination]]s of a relatively small number of simple concepts, just as words are combinations of letters. All [[truth]]s may be expressed as appropriate combinations of concepts, which can in turn be decomposed into simple ideas, rendering the analysis much easier. Therefore, this alphabet would provide a logic of invention, opposed to that of demonstration which was known so far. Since all sentences are composed of a [[Subject (grammar)|subject]] and a [[Predicate (grammar)|predicate]], one might
* Find all the predicates which are appropriate to a given subject, or
* Find all the subjects which are convenient to a given predicate.

For this, Leibniz was inspired in the {{lang |la |[[Ars Magna (Ramon Llull)|Ars Magna]]}} of [[Ramon Llull]], although he criticized this author because of the arbitrariness of his categories indexing.

Leibniz discusses in this work some [[combinatorial]] concepts. He had read [[Clavius|Clavius']] comments to [[Sacrobosco]]'s {{lang |la |[[De sphaera mundi]]}}, and some other contemporary works. He introduced the term {{lang |la |variationes ordinis}} for the [[permutation]]s, {{lang |la |combinationes}} for the combinations of two elements, ''con3nationes'' (shorthand for {{lang |la |conternationes}}) for those of three elements, etc. His general term for combinations was {{lang |la |complexions}}. He found the formula

:<math>{n \choose r} = {n-1\choose r} + {n-1\choose r-1}</math>

which he thought was original.

The first examples of use of his {{lang |la |ars combinatoria}}{{explain |date=September 2025}} are taken from law, the musical registry of an [[organ (music)|organ]], and the [[Aristotle|Aristotelian]] theory of generation of elements from the four primary qualities. But philosophical applications are of greater importance. He cites the idea of [[Thomas Hobbes]] that all reasoning is just a computation.

The most careful example is taken from geometry, from where we shall give some definitions. He introduces the Class I concepts, which are primitive.

;Class I: 1 point, 2 space, 3 included, [...] 9 parts, 10 total, [...] 14 number, 15 various [...]

Class II contains simple combinations.

;Class II.1: Quantity is 14 των 9

Where των means "of the" (from {{langx|grc|[[wikt:τῶν|τῶν]]}}). Thus, "Quantity" is the number of the parts. Class III contains the ''con3nationes'':

;Class III.1: Interval is 2.3.10

Thus, "Interval" is the space included in total. Of course, concepts deriving from former classes may also be defined.

;Class IV.1: Line is 1/3 των 1

Where 1/3 means the first concept of class III. Thus, a "line" is the interval of (between) points.

Leibniz compares his system to the [[Chinese language|Chinese]] and [[Egyptian language]]s, although he did not really understand them at this point. For him, this is a first step towards the {{lang |la |[[Characteristica Universalis]]}}, the [[perfect language]] which would provide a direct representation of ideas along with a calculus for philosophical reasoning.

As a preface, the work begins with a [[proof of the existence of God]], cast in geometrical form, and based on the [[argument from motion]].
